analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Fatality rates reported in South Asia range between 40 and 75 per cent. Survivors may suffer long-term neurological complications, including memory loss, personality changes, and difficulty concentrating.

analysis.brief_en: The article explains the Nipah virus, emphasizing its transmission routes and the importance of prevention in Bangladesh. The Nipah virus is not new to the country, with repeated cases almost every year, particularly in winter. It is primarily spread through raw date palm sap contaminated by bat saliva or urine, and can also spread through close contact with infected animals or via bodily fluids in human-to-human transmission. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and can escalate to encephalitis, with fatality rates ranging between 40 and 75 per cent in South Asia. Survivors may face long-term neurological issues. The article highlights that while Nipah does not spread easily through casual contact or air travel, authorities have increased airport screening as a precaution. Prevention measures include avoiding raw or fermented date palm sap, washing fruits thoroughly, and seeking medical attention after possible exposure. The focus is on awareness and consistent prevention rather than panic.

This case comes after two infections were detected in neighboring India, prompting several Asian countries to increase health screenings at airports.
